headline_marked: US [[launches new Iran strikes, reimposes naval blockade]]
headline: US launches new Iran strikes, reimposes naval blockade
summary: President Donald Trump warns of targeting power plants and bridges if Tehran does not negotiate, as tensions escalate in the Gulf.
details: US forces carried out strikes against Iran for a fourth consecutive day on Tuesday, while simultaneously reimposing a naval blockade to prevent ships from entering or leaving Iranian ports.
President Donald Trump stated that strikes will expand next week to target power plants and bridges if Tehran does not agree to a deal, warning that it will get "really bad for them."
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the strikes aimed to degrade Iranian capabilities used to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical channel for global oil and gas.
Iranian state media reported explosions near the port city of Bandar Abbas and on Qeshm island. In response, Iran launched a drone attack on a US military base in Jordan.
The renewed naval blockade has been described by Iranian officials as a move that dismantled a previous peace memorandum. At least 28 people have been killed in Iran since last week.
Iran also targeted US allies in the region, firing missiles and drones at Bahrain and Jordan. Bahrain reported intercepting several attacks, while Jordan shot down four Iranian missiles.
The conflict has extended to commercial shipping, with Iran hitting two ships in the Strait of Hormuz and a Norwegian tanker being hit by an unidentified device off the Oman coast.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Iran that Israel would deal a 'decisive blow' if the country were attacked, speaking from Dimona, a site linked to Israel's nuclear arsenal.
caption:
US forces strike Iran for a fourth day in a row and reimpose a naval blockade. Trump warns power plants and bridges are next.

US forces carried out strikes against Iran for a fourth consecutive day on Tuesday, while simultaneously reimposing a naval blockade to prevent ships from entering or leaving Iranian ports.

President Donald Trump stated that strikes will expand next week to target power plants and bridges if Tehran does not agree to a deal, warning that it will get "really bad for them."

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the strikes aimed to degrade Iranian capabilities used to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical channel for global oil and gas.

Iranian state media reported explosions near the port city of Bandar Abbas and on Qeshm island. In response, Iran launched a drone attack on a US military base in Jordan.

The renewed naval blockade has been described by Iranian officials as a move that dismantled a previous peace memorandum. At least 28 people have been killed in Iran since last week.

Iran also targeted US allies in the region, firing missiles and drones at Bahrain and Jordan. Bahrain reported intercepting several attacks, while Jordan shot down four Iranian missiles.

The conflict has extended to commercial shipping, with Iran hitting two ships in the Strait of Hormuz and a Norwegian tanker being hit by an unidentified device off the Oman coast.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Iran that Israel would deal a 'decisive blow' if the country were attacked, speaking from Dimona, a site linked to Israel's nuclear arsenal.

headline_marked: Tax cut, but [[SIM card prices remain high]]
headline: Tax cut, but SIM card prices remain high
summary: Despite the government removing a 300 Taka tax on mobile SIMs, consumers are still paying 200 to 400 Taka for new connections.
details: The government completely withdrew a 300 Taka tax on mobile SIMs in the national budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year, resulting in a revenue loss of approximately 1,200 crore Taka for the state.
Despite the tax removal, new prepaid SIMs are still being sold for between 200 and 400 Taka. Grameenphone's prepaid SIMs are mostly 400 Taka, while Robi's are 200 Taka and Banglalink's are 400 Taka.

Mobile operators explain that the final price is not just about tax. It includes costs for the SIM chip, plastic, packaging, transport, distributor and retailer commissions, and customer registration expenses.
Operators also add bundled data, minutes, and SMS to new SIMs, which adds to the cost. Some operators also use different pricing strategies to attract new customers based on their market share.
Operators claim they were previously subsidizing SIM sales. They argue that when the 300 Taka tax was active, the total cost to activate a new SIM was between 550 and 600 Taka.

Grameenphone stated that some old stock is still in the market and they plan to introduce more affordable SIMs within two to three weeks. Banglalink has already reduced the price of its 'Rise' SIM for youth by 33%.
According to BTRC statistics, there are nearly 19 crore active mobile subscribers in Bangladesh, with 28 lakh new users added in the last three months.
caption:
The government cut a 300 Taka tax on SIM cards, but are you still paying the same price?

The government completely withdrew a 300 Taka tax on mobile SIMs in the national budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year, resulting in a revenue loss of approximately 1,200 crore Taka for the state.

Despite the tax removal, new prepaid SIMs are still being sold for between 200 and 400 Taka. Grameenphone's prepaid SIMs are mostly 400 Taka, while Robi's are 200 Taka and Banglalink's are 400 Taka.

Mobile operators explain that the final price is not just about tax. It includes costs for the SIM chip, plastic, packaging, transport, distributor and retailer commissions, and customer registration expenses.

Operators also add bundled data, minutes, and SMS to new SIMs, which adds to the cost. Some operators also use different pricing strategies to attract new customers based on their market share.

Operators claim they were previously subsidizing SIM sales. They argue that when the 300 Taka tax was active, the total cost to activate a new SIM was between 550 and 600 Taka.

Grameenphone stated that some old stock is still in the market and they plan to introduce more affordable SIMs within two to three weeks. Banglalink has already reduced the price of its 'Rise' SIM for youth by 33%.

According to BTRC statistics, there are nearly 19 crore active mobile subscribers in Bangladesh, with 28 lakh new users added in the last three months.
